case_name: Lakshmi Precision Screws Limited v Ram Bahagat
respondent:
Ram Bahagat
Supreme Court of India

13 August 2002
Appeal (civil) 4964 of 2002
The Judgment was delivered by : Umesh C. Banerjee, J.
Leave granted.
1. Relying upon the well-accepted and settled principles of law as regards the norm of interference with the order of inferior Tribunals, the High Court negated the plea of the Appellant herein that Certified Standing Order being a part of the conditions of service, ought to be strictly interpreted and there is no scope of reading into the same, some other element. It is in this score the decision of this Court in Syed Yakoob (Syed Yakoob v. K.S. Radhakrishnan &
facts: The petitioner company engaged Ram Bahagat, the respondent-workman as a Helper on 08 December 1980.
On 6 November 1989 he was promoted as Operator.
For the discharge of his duties against the post of Operator, he was deputed to work in the elector-plating unit of the factory.
He continued to work till 12 October 1990 and thereafter absented himself without any prior information with effect from 13 October 1990
The respondent-workman did not comply with the condition stipulated in the letter dated 17 October 1990

A perusal of the aforesaid letter shows that the aforesaid action had been taken u/cl. 9(f) (ii) of the Certified Standing Orders of the Company, in view of the fact that the respondent-workman had remained absent from duty for a period of 10 days continuously.
The respondent-workman is stated to have refused to receive the registered communication dated 25 October 1990.
He, however, addressed a letter dated 30 January 1991 requesting the management to take him back on duty.
In this behalf, he also enclosed his medical certificate as also a fitness certificate.
issues: Can it be said to be within the jurisdiction of this Court u/art. 136 of the Constitution to intervene or interfere with an appraisal of evidence on record ?

A further question also in consequence thereof arises that in the event the High Court records a finding in terms of the order of the Tribunal and in the event of a party being aggrieved, would there be an inevitable refusal of this Court to entertain
petitioner_arguments: The Action of the management in terminating the services of the respondent- workman was not justified
He made a reference of the earlier letter dated 24 October 1990 sent by him to the management, requesting for leave on medical grounds.
court_reasoning: The jurisdiction conferred on the High Courts under Art. 226 to issue a writ of certiorari can be legitimately exercised.

A finding of fact recorded by the Tribunal cannot be challenged in proceedings for a writ of certiorari on the ground that the relevant and material evidence adduced before the Tribunal was insufficient or inadequate

The law is well settled to the effect that finding of the Labour Court cannot be challenged in a proceeding in a writ of certiorari on the ground that the relevant and material evidence adduced before the Labour Court was insufficient or inadequate though, however, perversity of the order would warrant intervention of the High Court.
holding: The request of the respondent-workman for being taken back on duty was declined.
The Action of the management in terminating the services of the respondent- workman was not justified and thus ordered his reinstatement with continuity in service along with 67% back wages
